mcqs.question: A class has a method reachable from outside the package purely so its own subclasses can use it internally. What's the risk of leaving it public?
options: External callers will eventually depend on it, turning an implementation detail into a de facto contract
The method will run slower than if it were private
The compiler will refuse to build the class
Subclasses will no longer be able to call the method
mcqs.explanation: Anything reachable gets used eventually — callers don't know or care that a public method was 'only meant for subclasses.' Visibility has no effect on runtime speed, doesn't block compilation, and doesn't stop subclasses from calling it either.

mcqs.question: Which of these changes to a public method is breaking, not additive-safe?
options: Adding a new optional parameter with a default value
Adding a new public method alongside the existing ones
Adding a new field to a response object that callers weren't reading before
Changing what type an existing parameter accepts
mcqs.explanation: Changing an existing parameter's accepted type changes behavior for every current call site — a breaking change. A new optional parameter with a default, a new method, and a new response field are all additive: existing callers, unmodified, keep compiling and behaving the same.

mcqs.question: You need to add a timeout option to a widely-used public method and expect to add more optional settings later. Which approach scales best?
options: Add the new setting as a required parameter
Bundle current and future optional settings into an options object parameter
Publish a new major version every time you add a setting
Overload the method for every possible combination of settings
mcqs.explanation: An options object absorbs new optional settings without another signature change or breaking release each time. A required parameter breaks every caller immediately; a major version per setting is needless churn; overloading for every combination grows combinatorially and quickly becomes unmanageable.

mcqs.question: A public getter returns a class's internal mutable list directly. A caller removes an item from the returned list. What actually happens?
options: Nothing — the returned list is always a copy by default in most languages
The caller's removal has no effect on the class's internal state
The class's internal list is modified too, since the caller holds a reference to the same object
The removal throws a runtime error because the list is read-only
mcqs.explanation: Returning the internal object by reference means the caller holds the exact same list the class uses internally — mutating it from outside silently changes the class's own state and can break its invariants. Most mainstream languages don't copy collections by default on return, and nothing here is read-only unless the class deliberately made it so.
